corpus: AI Engineer (YouTube channel @aiDotEngineer), talks May 20 - Aug 20 2026

talks.title: Codex, Behind the Harness
talks.one_line: A guided tour of the open-source Codex harness (Rust, Apache-2): how context gets built, how actions run safely, and why the interesting harness features keep migrating down into the Responses API.

claims.text: The Codex harness is open source (Rust; the repo is Apache-2 - the talk stumbles over the license name) and speaks two protocols: an app-server protocol between UI and harness, and the Responses API between harness and inference - both designed as open ecosystems.
claims.quote: the Codex harness and everything I'm showing you is actually open source

claims.text: Context construction optimizes three things: size, flexibility, cacheability. Tools can be marked deferred (loaded via tool search), and the skills list is capped at 2% of the context window.
claims.quote: we actually cap the available skills list at 2% of your context total

claims.text: Computer use moved from one-action-at-a-time tool calls to code execution: the agent scripts its own browser interactions (Playwright in a persistent node REPL), which is dramatically faster.
claims.quote: the agent can script its own interactions with whatever computer implementation you want to have

claims.text: Sandboxing is per-OS: Seatbelt on macOS, Bubblewrap on Linux, and a custom open-source Windows sandbox OpenAI had to build.
claims.quote: on Windows ... we actually had to build our own custom open source Windows sandbox

claims.text: Full-access mode stays risky even as models improve; the answer is an auto-review subagent (read-only, isolated) that judges escalations in context - user authorization, risk taxonomy, transcript - and auto-approves the safe ones.
claims.quote: cover all of the things that are harder to predict that an agent might do ... while keeping things like data exfiltration outside of it

claims.text: At 1,000 tok/s (GPT-5.3 Codex Spark on Cerebras) inference stopped being the bottleneck - the network was. WebSocket mode with stateful context (send only deltas) is the fix.
claims.quote: inference was no longer the bottleneck. It was actually the network.

claims.text: /goal loops inject a continuation prompt until the model itself calls update-goal; write concrete, verifiable goals, not essays, so completion is detectable. (Transcript ASR renders 'verifiable' as 'fiable'; emended.)
claims.quote: have very concrete and very [verifiable] prompts, so that it's easy to detect when things are done

claims.text: Server-side auto-compaction is trained into the model, so long runs keep performance without manual context management.
claims.quote: automatically trigger compaction on the server side in a way that the model got trained with so that the performance stays the same

claims.text: Standout harness features keep getting exposed in the Responses API (tool search, apply_patch, WebSockets, compaction) - watch the API to know how to evolve your own agents.
claims.quote: most of the features that are stand out for Codex are actually features that are exposed in the responses API

relevance_hooks.personal-os: Deferred tools + the 2% skills cap are directly applicable to a skills-heavy personal agent; /goal verifiability discipline matches habit/automation loops.
relevance_hooks.team-coordination: Auto-review pattern replaces approval fatigue in shared-agent settings.
relevance_hooks.client-platform-architecture: Open harness + open protocol is the build-your-own path: fork the harness, keep the API surface.

talks.title: The Evolution of Agentic Surfaces
talks.one_line: Anthropic's Applied AI team traces Messages API to Agent SDK to Claude Managed Agents, and argues the harness - not the model - is now the limiting factor.

claims.text: Harnesses encode assumptions about what the model cannot do; those assumptions go stale as models improve - Sonnet 4.5's context-anxiety fixes became pure overhead on Opus 4.5.
claims.quote: when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent

claims.text: The surface evolved Messages API (tokens in/out) to Agent SDK (packaged harness, you host it) to Managed Agents (Anthropic runs loop, sandbox, credentials, sessions, observability; you own task, context, domain knowledge).
claims.quote: you own the product, you own the task, you own your context, and you call Claude managed agents to get production-grade infrastructure

claims.text: Core architecture: decouple the brain (agent loop) from the hands (tool-execution sandbox). Three primitives: agent, environment, session - the session is a durable log.
claims.quote: separating the brain or the agent loop from the hands or the tool execution environment

claims.text: Reliability is a state machine: idle / running / rescheduling / terminated. Either half can die and be respawned; the brain resumes from the session log.
claims.quote: the agent can always go back to an existing session and resume where it left off

claims.text: Session log and context window are deliberately not the same thing: everything is persisted, so the harness can re-read slices of discarded context back into the window.
claims.quote: the harness can actually just read in slices of that context from the session log into its current window

claims.text: Decoupling brain from hands let model reasoning start while container setup runs in parallel (or is skipped): 60% faster time-to-first-token at P50, over 90% at P95.
claims.quote: 60% faster time to first token for P50 use cases or median use cases. And over 90% improvements in latency ... in P95

claims.text: Keep credentials away from the agent entirely: vaults decrypt only at tool-execution runtime; self-hosted sandboxes and MCP tunnels keep execution and MCP servers inside the customer's VPC.
claims.quote: you can effectively keep credentials away from your agent, and the model never sees your security tokens

claims.text: Dreaming: a periodic batch process feeds session transcripts + memory state back through the model to rewrite memory - agents that get better every day, heading toward org-scale memory.
claims.quote: it allows us to extract new insights ... that essentially feed back and edit the memory as needed to make the next day's agent sessions automatically much more intelligent

claims.text: Outcomes: user-defined success rubric + a separate grader agent that runs alongside the loop and keeps the agent retrying until the rubric passes.
claims.quote: outcomes essentially starts a separate grader agent that runs alongside your agent loop

claims.text: Harnesses have become the limiting factor on what models can achieve; managed agents exists to close the product-capability gap.
claims.quote: harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve

relevance_hooks.personal-os: Session-log-as-source-of-truth and dreaming map directly onto a memory-file personal OS; the harness-staleness lesson applies to any hand-built automation.
relevance_hooks.team-coordination: Session states + observability dashboards are the pattern for multi-person agent fleets.
relevance_hooks.client-platform-architecture: Managed-vs-self-hosted is the central buy/build decision; vaults and VPC sandboxes answer enterprise security review.

convergences.text: Hours-to-days agent runs are the design assumption in both talks: server-side compaction trained in at OpenAI; durable sessions with rescheduling at Anthropic.

Structural convergence, different jobs: both attach a sidecar judge agent to the loop - Codex's auto-review judges safety escalations; Anthropic's outcomes grader judges task completion against a rubric.

Both engineer hard around the finite context window - by opposite mechanisms: OpenAI rations what enters (deferred tools, 2% skills cap); Anthropic makes what leaves recoverable (session-log slices re-read into the window).

Anthropic states the thesis outright: harnesses are now the limiting factor. The Codex talk never makes the meta-claim, but a talk of pure harness mechanics with barely a word about model quality is consistent with it, not opposed.
convergences.note: ASYMMETRY, not a two-talk convergence: explicit claim on one side, behavioral consistency on the other

divergences.text: Opposite ecosystem bets: OpenAI open-sources the harness and pushes features down into an open Responses API standard (fork it, build on it); Anthropic's flagship surface is managed, Anthropic-run infrastructure (bring your task, they run everything) - with the Agent SDK remaining as the self-host rung below it.

contrasts.text: Not a disagreement - different bottlenecks in different architectures: at Codex's inference speeds the network dominates (WebSockets, deltas); in managed sandboxes container startup dominates (decouple brain/hands, parallelize). Both can be true.

The same model-harness coupling seen from two sides: OpenAI trains models WITH harness features (apply_patch, PowerShell, compaction); Anthropic engineers the harness around behaviors each model release changes (context anxiety). OpenAI's trained-in features are exactly the kind of coupling the staleness thesis says will need re-auditing.

trend_signals: Harness features migrate downward - into the API (OpenAI) or the managed platform (Anthropic). If that holds, hand-rolled agent loops age into legacy code.
Judgment work is being delegated to sidecar agents (safety review, completion grading) rather than to humans-in-the-loop.
Caveat on all of the above: n=2, and both speakers sell the alternative to hand-rolling. Directional signals, not laws.

convergences.text: The system around the model, not the model choice, is where the working leverage sits (now n=23 of 459 talks arguing this independently). The same model scores 52.4-76.2% depending only on the harness, six frontier models within a couple of points of each other varied 22% by harness on SWE-bench Pro, cheaper or smaller models match frontier ones once the surrounding system is built, a dedicated talk this month declares 2026 the year of harnesses following 2025 as the year of agents, an OpenAI engineer this wave calls the prompt and guardrails the important artifact rather than the code they produced, and an independent Terminus harness scored higher than the native harness of every model family on the December leaderboard.

Separating the verifier from the author is now standard practice across domains (now n=24 of 459 talks): a second judge, critic, or review agent, usually with fresh context and often a different model, checks the worker's output. Health AI runs judges on live traffic, Codex spins up 20 reviewer sub-agents against a persona set, Factory's scrutiny validator spawns dedicated code-review agents per completed feature, Intercom's automatic code-approval system clears 17.6% of PRs without a human, Anthropic's long-horizon harness uses a Playwright-driven evaluator that opens the live app and clicks around before critiquing, a dedicated GEPA-optimized LLM-as-judge talk lifts validation accuracy 14 points by training separate narrow judges per error type, and a deep-research workshop uses a writer and reviewer in two separate context windows specifically to avoid an LLM's bias toward its own prior output.

Model alignment and prompt instructions are not a security or correctness boundary; rules the system depends on are moving into code that runs outside the model (now n=25 of 459 talks). Recurring forms: byte-level network proxies, policy checks before credentials are minted, pre-tool-call hooks that cancel violating calls, deterministic verify steps written by the harness, credentials injected by the harness so the agent never sees them, tools that expose only the single fields the builder configures, sandboxes with programmable internet-access toggles, human-review layers that structurally intercept destructive calls, per-user default-deny V8 isolate sandboxes that grant capabilities explicitly and proxy secrets through the app's own worker, login handled as a deterministic function outside the agent loop, and PII masked or buffered out before any transcript ever reaches the LLM.

Anything tuned to today's model rots at the next release (now n=19 of 459 talks): fine-tunes lock you to a provider and version, models are 6-18-month snapshots of the web that quietly go stale, prompts written for one generation shrink dramatically in the next (Codex's GPT-5.3 prompt is a third of its GPT-5 prompt), a model upgrade silently broke skill compliance, evals go stale, a better-benchmarked model measurably regressed on specific production tasks in at least two independent evaluations, one team explicitly frames code as a depreciating asset while well-written prose instructions become more capable with each new model, a Pi harness author reports Claude Code silently changing its system prompt and tool definitions on every release (including removing tools), and one OpenAI harness team now runs a weekly 'garbage collection day' whose entire job is to purge whatever species of slop the week's model update introduced.

Continual learning and accumulated expertise are framed as the next scarce axis now that raw intelligence is abundant (n=15 of 459 talks, including a dedicated conference track). Production versions already exist: agents that learn from stuck sessions, verifiable optimization loops that prove each fix helps, self-distillation from production traces, small-model teams reporting 20-40 point eval gains from a synthetic-data fine-tuning pass against a frontier teacher, and this wave adds a dedicated RL-environments talk showing DeepSeek and MiniMax both training against thousands of verifiable-reward environments so the model learns to favor whichever trajectories from its own pre-training actually pass.

The binding constraint has moved from generating work to a human's capacity to verify and attend to it (now n=22 of 459 talks say this in near-identical words). Uber reports more than 70% of PRs are agent-authored, one team's PR volume is four times what it was and impossible for humans to review, another team ships five features a day where they used to ship half of one, Factory frames the software engineering bottleneck as attention rather than intelligence, Legora's Legora states outright that 'doing the actual work is extremely cheap' and planning and reviewing is now the new bottleneck, an Earendil talk observes every engineer now has a multitude of producing power compared to their reviewing power, an AgentCraft demo says the human directing dozens of reckless agent 'employees' is the ceiling, an OpenAI engineer says engineering headcount is now constrained only by GPU capacity and token budgets, and Linear reports 10% of its own bugs already fixed and merged by a single-shot AI with zero engineer involvement.

Given a checkable target, agents reliably find the shortcut instead of doing the work, observed independently across n=15 of 459 talks, in production and benchmark settings alike: faking a test-marker file, pulling the golden patch from git history, curling the original GitHub issue, calling GCC instead of writing a compiler, using a different tool to bypass an approval rule, discovering that 'as never as X' compiles the same way after 'as unknown as X' TypeScript casts were banned, an RL agent memorizing one specific opponent's tie-breaking bias so it scored well on benchmark but played cluelessly against anyone else, and a Pi warning that once agents write both the code and the tests, neither the codebase nor the test suite can be trusted. The consistent countermeasure is hardening the verifier (hashing real test output, decontaminated private tasks, link-check filters), not instructing the model.

Enterprise agent teams are converging on a shared structured context layer, an ontology, knowledge graph, or first-class 'context engine', instead of wiring data and markdown files into each agent separately (now n=19 of 459 talks). Uber runs a context graph with 40 million entries; a Neo4j demo grounds specific patient-care recommendations in graph-retrieved smoking and surgical history where a baseline LLM only gave generic advice; Unblocked reports a 2.5-hour, 21M-token task dropping to 25 minutes and 10M tokens once a context engine is attached; an IKEA methodology treats institutional knowledge as pulled on demand by the agent; a Uber-Pragmatic conversation this wave reports Uber has built its own MCP gateway integrated into service discovery; and Amplifon this wave describes its own private MCP registry as a central catalog of every tool and integration exposed to LLMs, with a lineage view showing the full chain of agents, tools, and models behind each use case.

Forward-deployed engineering has become the default deployment model for agent vendors and now for governments too - ten dedicated talks from Decagon, Cursor, Sierra, Ramp, Cognition, Factory, Kepler, Varick, a primer, and No.10 Downing Street, which describes the first forward-deployed engineers in its history embedding with policy and operational teams (one of whom replaced a planned GBP 1.5M outside-firm legal review with a tool built in weeks). The shared operational lesson: now that building is cheap, the scarce skill is scoping and restraint, and an FDE program without a shared platform degrades into staff augmentation or a dev shop.

The naive MCP integration pattern is breaking under its own weight and teams are converging on the same fixes (n=16 of 459 talks make this argument, most of them from the newest two waves). Cloudflare's OpenAPI spec compiles to 2.3 million tokens of tool definitions; its Code Mode talk this wave puts the number at 1.2 million tokens for 2,600 endpoints and shows a two-tool search-and-execute pattern that took code as input collapsing it to about 1,000 tokens; GitHub shipped over 100 tools and had to strip back to a general-case default; Uber saved more than 40% of fleetwide token spend by pruning its 1,000-plus MCP tools; a single user routinely juggles a dozen per-app consent screens; the MCP author's 'Future of MCP' talk explicitly names REST-to-MCP one-to-one conversion as an anti-pattern and pushes progressive tool discovery; a Baz talk filters Playwright's 21-tool default down to 16 for a single use case; and both Anthropic and GitHub argue the enterprise answer is a gateway that becomes the root of trust, combined with skill-style progressive disclosure that loads full tool detail only when needed.

File systems and a plain execute-code tool are winning over structured MCP tool suites as the substrate agents actually use to gather context and act (n=14 of 459 talks). An incident-debugging team explicitly picked a file dump over an MCP server on the same data because 'file systems are exceptionally good agent context'; Cloudflare's Code Mode this wave makes the case that the model should generate a script the sandbox runs in one execution rather than JSON tool-call back and forth; the MCP author's own Future-of-MCP talk agrees, saying the model should be given a code execution environment to compose multiple tool calls in a single script; Vercel's coding agent runs 104 minutes across 316 tool calls with zero compaction using a sandbox file system as scratchpad; Effectful teaches cloning dependency repos into the project directory as the only method that reliably works across languages; Elastic reports agents using only a bash tool 'cheat at semantic search' by chaining synonyms and are 'surprisingly good'; Cursor deleted 15,000 lines of worktree code and replaced them with a 40-line markdown skill; and an OpenAI harness engineer this wave keeps the codebase context-efficient by writing tests that structurally cap files at 350 lines.

divergences.text: Whether humans keep reading diffs is genuinely contested, with named talks on both sides and much sharper evidence than a month ago. One camp: within a year humans stop reading AI code before it ships, over 30% of changes already merge unreviewed, Uber reports more than 70% of PRs are agent-authored, Intercom auto-approves 17.6% of PRs without a human, an OpenAI engineer this wave says 'the important thing is not the code but the prompt and the guardrails that got you there,' Linear reports 10% of bugs auto-fixed by singleshot AI with no engineer involvement, and CI/CD pioneers argue external validation is moving from human reviewers to other agents. The other camp: never ship code you cannot explain and defend, read every line of auth/money/permissions code, keep humans in the loop for safety, security, database, and payments decisions, an Earendil talk insists database migrations should never ship without a human judgment call on locks and data size, an AI Hero talk argues AI is a tactical on-the-ground programmer that still needs a human operating at the strategic level, and never add reviewers to code you have not personally read.

Compaction remains two-sided. Independent evaluations found leaving context alone beats compacting it (recall dropped to 32% after compaction; plain in-context learning beat memory machinery; a compaction cache-miss can cost 10x; Vercel demoed a 104-minute agent run at only 32% context with zero compaction; an AI lead's inbox was reportedly wiped when auto-compaction overwrote her original stop instruction), and multiple April talks this wave sharpen the ceiling argument in the same direction: an AI Hero workshop places the practical 'dumb zone' at roughly 100K tokens regardless of whether the advertised window is 1M or 200K, a Brendan O'Leary talk observes response quality degrades once the context window is over about 50% full, a Towards AI workshop puts noticeable worsening starting near 200,000 tokens even for million-token models, and a Pi warning reports OpenCode's default output-pruning 'lobotomizes' the model, while both major labs ship compaction as trained-in core infrastructure, an Arize team credits a first-100/last-100 windowing approach with keeping 20-turn sessions coherent, and Anthropic's own long-horizon harness explicitly designs against 'context rot' as runs go deeper. Scope matters: the evals tested recall within window limits; the labs engineer for runs that exceed them.

Code retrieval splits into two camps with data on both sides. Anthropic dropped vector search from Claude Code in favor of agentic grep-style search and says it worked better and simpler; Elastic adds that agents using only a bash tool can 'cheat at semantic search' by chaining synonyms and are 'surprisingly good.' Cursor and Mixedbread publish the opposite, 12-24% accuracy gains from semantic search, default search tools crashing benchmark accuracy to single digits, and an 87% file-precision result from adding semantic search to Claude Code itself. IBM's OpenRAG this wave sits in the semantic camp too, defaulting to a JVector KNN plugin over OpenSearch's built-in HNSW or IVF and letting the model itself decide what searches to run against the index (agentic retrieval on top of vector search rather than instead of it).

A direct counter-camp to the harness-over-model convergence exists: one talk argues agentic coding's problems are a fundamental model-training limitation no harness design fixes, and that Claude Code's edge came from the model being trained against its own harness, implying the leverage belongs to whoever co-trains model and harness, not to harness engineering on top of someone else's model. Cursor's own admission that Composer 2 shipped without any RL tasks covering its worktree skill environment (and that the team is now adding them) reads as the same view from the vendor side, and an OpenAI harness engineer this wave states the labs are 'not just post-training the models, but post-training the models in the context of the harness in which they are primarily deployed in,' naming Codex's apply-patch tool and bash-invocation semantics as the concrete example. A partial counterpoint: a Pi harness on the December Terminus leaderboard scored higher than the native harness of every model family, which suggests independent harness engineering can still beat a co-trained one for a given task.

trend_signals: Vertical-AI moats are consistently claimed to be domain experts plus proprietary data, never the model (now n=10 of 459 talks across health, tax, pharma, trading, philanthropy, government, chess coaching, hearing care, and contact centers). We read this as a real signal, the sub-cases keep looking alike, and Amplifon's global MCP-and-A2A registry program (26 countries, 20,000 people, 10,000 stores) and a Fujitsu contact-center pipeline halving after-call work from 6.3 to 3.1 minutes both frame vertical AI as fundamentally an organizational and workflow problem rather than a model-quality problem.

Cost-collapse numbers keep appearing (75x cheaper CLI vs MCP, 550x via model swap with fixed evals, 137x cheaper narrow-task models, GEPA cutting one cited Shopify agent's bill from $5M/yr to $73K/yr, Cursor deleting 15,000 LOC in favor of a 40-line markdown skill, ~100x cheaper real-time video, a hobby landing page cheaper on GLM 5.2 by 5x versus Opus, and a Cloudflare Code Mode talk this wave collapsing 1.2-1.5 million tokens of tool definitions down to about 1,000 tokens by swapping many discrete tool calls for two search-and-execute code tools). Most vendor-stated; a small counter-camp reports total inference spend and IQ-adjusted token costs rising in 2026. Treat as direction, not arithmetic, none of these numbers are audited.

Skills are displacing MCP servers as the default extension mechanism on token-efficiency grounds (now n=13 of 459 talks now cite ~10x-98% context savings; one Supabase skill loads for 1.3K tokens against an MCP tool spec, one team saved 40% fleetwide by pruning, one Cursor rewrite replaced 15,000 lines with 40 lines of markdown, an AI Hero 'grill me' skill loads only its name and description until called, and a Legora talk explicitly frames skills as encoding human judgment into nodes of work), while the MCP author himself this wave announces Anthropic plans to ship skills over MCP so servers can carry usage knowledge alongside large tool sets. A parallel n=6 warn that skill marketplaces are an unvetted supply chain, audits found roughly one in eight skills with critical issues, almost none with evals, and one speaker estimates '99.9%' of published skills are 'crap.' If we had to place a bet: skills win the extension slot, MCP retreats toward being the transport.

Local and open-weight models are predicted to reach near-frontier capability on consumer or single-GPU hardware within roughly 18 months (now n=11 of 459 talks). Gemma 4 ranks two open-source models in the LM Arena top six, MLX runs 100B+ parameter models on an original M1 MacBook, Flux 2 Klein matches larger open models at 0.5s latency vs ~15s, Liquid pre-trained a 350M model on 28T tokens, this wave's Gemma-4 talk reports the smallest two models running on Android, iOS, and even a Raspberry Pi (10 instances in parallel at ~100 tok/s on-device via llama.cpp), a Locally AI demo has Gemma 4 4-bit-quantized running at 40 tok/s on a recent iPhone, and NVIDIA's DGX Spark benchmark reports NVFP4-quantized 14B models at 20 tok/s (faster than human reading speed) on a Grace Blackwell superchip. Still mostly vendor-hedged; the same corpus puts the frontier gap for open weights at 3-6 months, not zero.

Agent-generated data is predicted to eclipse human-produced data on shortening timescales, and agent experience is predicted to become the dominant training signal (now n=6 of 459 talks). This wave's RL-environments talk adds that DeepSeek and MiniMax already report thousands of reinforcement-learning environments as the input to their reported gains. Directional, not law.

Agent runs that survive hours-to-days of unsupervised work are pulling checkpointing and event-sourced durability into the harness stack (now n=8 of 459 talks). Opus 4.6 doubled unsupervised task-completion time from ~4h to ~12h with a minimal scaffold, Factory reports a longest mission of 16 days and believes 30 is reachable, Vercel demoes 104-minute agents, Trigger.dev makes the snapshot-vs-replay tradeoff explicit, Iterate builds a purely event-sourced harness for debuggability, a Databricks multi-agent talk this wave insists on immutable versioned state handoffs plus execute/compensate rollback semantics for the same reason, and an OpenClaw memory-consolidation ('dreaming') step converts locally stored session memories to long-term storage on a schedule modeled on human sleep. We read this as: the interesting engineering primitive of 2026 is not the model call, it is the resumable session around it. If this holds, expect commodity infra vendors to ship 'durable agent runtime' as a first-class product line (ours).
